Here you go. Run these as `master@` — which is already your active account, so no switch needed.

**Verify who you are first:**

```sh
gcloud config get-value account   # expect master@cyccommunitysailing.org
```

**1. Organization Administrator on the org:**

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 307534406562 \
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" \
  --condition=None
```

**2. Owner on the project:**

```sh
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding cyc-admin-scripts \
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --role="roles/owner" \
  --condition=None
```

**Verify both landed:**

```sh
gcloud organizations get-iam-policy 307534406562 \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" \
  --filter="bindings.members:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --format="value(bindings.role)"

gcloud projects get-iam-policy cyc-admin-scripts \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" \
  --filter="bindings.members:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --format="value(bindings.role)"
```

You should see `organizationAdmin` from the first and `owner` plus the three existing roles from the second.

**One thing to watch.** `ungood@onetrue.name` is outside `cyccommunitysailing.org`, and Google treats granting project **Owner** to an external user differently from other roles — it can send an invitation email to that address that must be accepted before the binding takes effect. If the second command succeeds but `get-iam-policy` doesn't show `owner`, check that inbox rather than re-running it. The org-level grant has no such flow.

`--condition=None` just suppresses the interactive condition prompt in recent gcloud.

If you'd rather these run right here so the output lands in the conversation, prefix with `!` — e.g. `! gcloud projects get-iam-policy cyc-admin-scripts ...`. I've deliberately not run the grants myself; they're outward-facing IAM changes and yours to make.

Neither grant is in place — the org-level one isn't there either, so that command either wasn't run or also failed.

**The org grant should work fine via CLI.** `ORG_MUST_INVITE_EXTERNAL_OWNERS` is specific to `roles/owner` on a project; nothing blocks `organizationAdmin` for an external principal. Worth re-running on its own:

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 307534406562 \
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" \
  --condition=None
```

**Project Owner is a genuine dead end via CLI.** This isn't a flag I can fix — Google refuses to grant `roles/owner` to a principal outside the organization through the API, full stop. There are two ways past it.

### Option A — console invitation (what I'd do)

Two minutes, and it gives you the single clean binding you asked for:

1. <https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/iam?project=cyc-admin-scripts>
2. **Grant access** → New principals: `ungood@onetrue.name`
3. Role: **Basic → Owner** → **Save**
4. Google emails an invitation to `ungood@onetrue.name`; accept it. The binding appears only after acceptance.

### Option B — skip Owner, grant the role set via CLI

Every *other* role grants to external principals without an invitation. So you can assemble Owner-equivalent access from the list the design doc already derived:

```sh
for role in \
  roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin roles/compute.admin roles/compute.osLogin \
  roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor roles/cloudsql.admin roles/servicenetworking.networksAdmin \
  roles/dns.admin roles/artifactregistry.admin roles/secretmanager.admin \
  roles/run.developer roles/cloudscheduler.admin \
  roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin roles/iam.roleAdmin roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin
do
  gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding cyc-admin-scripts \
    --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" --role="$role" --condition=None
done
```

The last three are what `packages/bootstrap` itself needs — creating service accounts, creating the custom role, and writing project IAM — none of which the scoped `deployer` role grants, deliberately.

**Worth knowing either way:** once the org grant lands, `organizationAdmin` carries `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`, which cascades to every project under the org. So you'll be able to grant yourself any project role except Owner without `master@`. Option B is really just doing that up front.

I'd take A — it's what you asked for, it's one binding instead of fourteen, and `projectIamAdmin` in option B is functionally Owner anyway, so B buys precision it doesn't really deliver.

Tree is clean and step 3's changes are intact. Thirteen commits.

## What the preview actually told us

**Step 3 is diff-neutral** — confirmed by running the preview both ways. My earlier reading was wrong; I corrected it above.

**Found and fixed a bug the worktree workflow guarantees** (`c7d4b0fa`). `pulumi` stores the selected stack per *directory path* in `~/.pulumi/workspaces/`. Your main checkout has `prod` selected; a fresh session worktree has nothing, so `just deploy`, `preview`, and `deploy-bootstrap` all died with `no stack selected`. Since CLAUDE.md mandates a worktree per session, every future session would have hit this. Now `--stack "${PULUMI_STACK:-prod}"` is explicit, which also removes hidden per-machine state from the deploy path.

**Pre-existing drift you should know about before applying anything:**

```
~ 1 to update    gcp:cloudrunv2:Job run-reports-job  [diff: ~template]
+-2 to replace   substrate-image, report-runner-image [diff: ~provider]
   88 unchanged
```

That's there on `main` too, unrelated to this branch — the `~provider` diff means the docker-build provider version moved, probably from a nix update. It'll rebuild and repush both images on the next apply. That's #114's complaint exactly.

**One thing the preview did *not* show**, and it matters: the three IAM bindings the console stripped from `ungood@` don't appear. Pulumi compares against last-known state, not live GCP, so out-of-band changes are invisible without `pulumi refresh` or `up --refresh`. Run a refresh before step 7 or the `retainOnDelete` work will be reasoning from a stale picture of what exists.

Also confirmed working end to end: `doctor` gates correctly, the podman machine starts, and the IAP tunnel reaches Cloud SQL at `10.159.0.3` — so `scripts/pulumi-tunnel` and `scripts/db-tunnel` are verified against real infrastructure, not just `bash -n`.

Diagnosis is clear, and there's genuinely good news buried in it:

**ADC now resolves to `ungood@onetrue.name`.** The impersonation is gone — that half worked, and it's the core of what #87 set out to fix.

**But the credentials are in the wrong place, and that's a trap waiting to spring.** The project-local `.gcloud/` exists (so something has loaded the new `.envrc` — it has gcloud's `gce` and survey files) but contains **no** `application_default_credentials.json` and no `configurations/`. Meanwhile your actual ADC sits at `~/.config/gcloud/`.

The moment direnv is fully live in your shell, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` will point at that missing project-local file. `google-auth-library` treats that variable as authoritative — it throws rather than falling back to the global path. So every Node tool and Pulumi would break, even though `gcloud` itself keeps working.

`just doctor` will catch it (`ADC credentials file is missing (…)` → `just auth-adc`), which is a decent validation of the preflight, but better to not get there.

**Fix — in your interactive shell, inside the worktree:**

```sh
cd /Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/worktrees/deployer-access
direnv reload
echo $CLOUDSDK_CONFIG        # must print .../isthmia/.gcloud — if empty, stop and tell me
just auth-gcp                # creates the isthmia config in the new location
just auth-adc                # writes ADC beside it
just doctor                  # expect: all checks pass, ADC identity = ungood@onetrue.name
```

`auth-gcp` matters as much as `auth-adc` here — the project-local dir has no `configurations/`, so gcloud has no `isthmia` configuration there and `doctor`'s configuration check will fail until you run it.

Once `doctor` is clean as `ungood@`, run `just deploy`. That's the step that actually proves #87: a full apply, as yourself, with no `master@` anywhere in the chain.

Confirmed from the audit log. Two `SetIAMPolicy` calls at **20:10:42–43 UTC** — that's exactly when `just deploy-bootstrap` ran, and the two resource IDs are our two service accounts.

**Our `bootstrap` apply removed `master@` and `ungood@` from `serviceAccountUser`**, even though the code uses additive `gcp.serviceaccount.IAMMember`. Note `serviceAccountTokenCreator` kept both members — only the role our new binding touched lost its existing ones. That's authoritative behaviour from a resource documented as additive.

Nothing is broken right now: both accounts hold project Owner, which includes `actAs`, so the lost bindings are functionally redundant today. And `just deploy` would recreate all five. But this matters a lot for what comes next.

**Steps 7–9 hand `bootstrap` ownership of exactly these bindings, while `infrastructure` still declares them.** We now have direct evidence that two stacks writing the same service-account IAM policy clobber each other. The plan assumed `IAMMember` was safely additive across stacks; it isn't, at least not here. So the migration is riskier than designed — and its `retainOnDelete` sequence is precisely a window where both stacks declare the same resource.

There's also a state complication: those five resources are now *absent* from `infrastructure`'s state, so step 7 can't mark them `retainOnDelete` — there's nothing there to mark.

Two ways forward:

**A. Restore, then migrate carefully.** `just deploy` to recreate the five, then steps 7–9 one at a time with a `preview` and a live IAM check between each. Faithful to the plan; slow; spends several applies re-creating bindings that step 10 deletes anyway.

**B. Converge directly.** Skip re-creating them. Do step 9 (delete the moved declarations from `infrastructure`) and step 10 (`deployers` → `deploy-runner`) — after which *neither* stack declares human bindings, and humans rely on Owner. That is the plan's designed end state, reached without the intermediate dance. Steps 7–8's `retainOnDelete`/`import` machinery only ever existed to avoid a gap the Owner grant has already made irrelevant for humans. The service accounts themselves still need the careful `import` treatment — that part of step 8 stands.

I'd take **B**. The `retainOnDelete` choreography was designed when the deployer's access depended on those bindings; it no longer does, and each extra apply is another chance for the clobbering we just observed.

Which way? If B, I'll rewrite steps 7–10 in the design doc first so the record matches what we actually did and why.

Migrate the service accounts and all project-level IAM from `packages/infrastructure` into `packages/bootstrap`. This collapses steps 7-10 of `.claude/plans/deployer-access.md` into one code change — read that doc for background, but this brief is the authority where they differ.

The previous commit already marked every moving resource `retainOnDelete: true` and applied it, so deleting these declarations hands the resources over instead of destroying them. Do not remove those `retainOnDelete` options from code you delete — you are deleting the whole declaration anyway.

## Move INTO `packages/bootstrap`

1. **`packages/infrastructure/src/service-account.ts`** — move the file. After this, `infrastructure` creates no service account and the file must not exist there.
2. **`substrate-runner`** (`compute.ts:24-31`) and **`report-runner`** (`run-reports-job.ts:21-27`) service accounts.
3. **`reportRunner.allowImpersonation(reportRunners)`** (`run-reports-job.ts:29`). Find where `reportRunners` is defined and move that list too.
4. **Three project IAM blocks**, all `gcp.projects.IAMMember`:
   - `compute.ts:33-41` — `substrate-runner` gets `logging.logWriter` and `monitoring.metricWriter`.
   - `compute.ts:44-58` — deployers get `iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` and `compute.osLogin`. The `dependsOn: iapApi` must become a dependency on an `enableService("iap.googleapis.com")` in `bootstrap`; add the equivalent of `infrastructure`'s `services.ts` helper, or inline the `gcp.projects.Service`, whichever is less code.
   - `run-reports-job.ts:~128` — deployers get `roles/run.developer`.

`bootstrap` must export `substrateRunner` and `reportRunner` with at least `email`, `member`, and `name` as stack outputs.

**Who the deployer bindings are for in `bootstrap`:** `deploy-runner` **and** `user:ungood@onetrue.name`. `deploy-runner` already holds `compute.osLogin`, `iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`, and `run.developer` through the predefined-role list in `deploy-runner.ts`, so do not duplicate those for it — just make sure the human is covered. Keep `ungood@` explicitly even though it holds project Owner: OS Login is demonstrably **not** covered by Owner for a principal outside the organization (this session hit exactly that failure), so dropping the explicit grant would break `just ssh`, `just logs`, `just db-tunnel`, and every deploy. Leave a one-line comment saying so. `master@` needs nothing — it has Owner and is break-glass only.

## Change IN `packages/infrastructure`

1. **New `src/identities.ts`** — one `pulumi.StackReference`, exporting typed `substrateRunner` and `reportRunner` objects with `email`, `member`, and `name`. The stack name comes from config (`bootstrapStack`) defaulting to `` `ungood/bootstrap/${pulumi.getStack()}` `` so the Pulumi organization is not hardcoded.
2. **Repoint every consumer** to import from `./identities` instead of `./compute` or the local constant. The full list, verified: `compute.ts:87`, `substrate.ts:5,26,33,35,45`, `portal.ts:3,24`, `directus.ts:5,52`, `run-reports-job.ts:38,80,126,151`.
3. **`config.ts:14`** — `deployers` becomes `["serviceAccount:deploy-runner@cyc-admin-scripts.iam.gserviceaccount.com"]`, with a comment saying human deployers get access through project `roles/owner` (see `docs/manual-setup.md` §7) rather than this list. It is still used by `artifact-repository.ts:29`, which stays.
4. **Keep `enableService("iap.googleapis.com")` in `compute.ts`** even though its `dependsOn` consumer moved — the VM still needs the API enabled.

## Must not change

Resource-scoped IAM stays in `infrastructure`: `artifact-repository.ts:29`, `substrate.ts:33-46`, and `Secret.grant` (`secret.ts`). Do not touch the VM, Cloud Run job, Cloud SQL, DNS, networking, or the docker images.

**Never use `gcp.projects.IAMPolicy` or `IAMBinding`, in either package.** Only additive `IAMMember`. An authoritative resource would delete `master@`'s `roles/owner`, which no code declares and which is the break-glass path into the project.

- `just ci` must pass, including `tsc --build` of both packages.
- `grep -rn "IAMPolicy\|IAMBinding" packages/` returns nothing.
- `packages/infrastructure/src/service-account.ts` no longer exists; nothing in `infrastructure` constructs a `ServiceAccount`.
- Do **not** run `pulumi preview`, `up`, or `import`. The `bootstrap` stack cannot resolve until the two accounts are imported into it, which I will do after your commit. A preview would fail and tell you nothing. Compile-time correctness is your acceptance bar — say so in your report.

**Deploy as `ungood@` succeeded** (4m21s) — `retainOnDelete` is in state, so the movers are now safe to remove from code.

The migration is running as one change instead of the plan's four steps, since you don't need the intermediate states preserved. One deliberate deviation from the plan, worth flagging: I'm keeping `ungood@` in the deployer SSH grants rather than dropping it for Owner as step 10 specified. This session proved Owner does **not** cover OS Login for an external principal — that's the `osLoginExternalUser` failure — so dropping it would break `ssh`, `logs`, `db-tunnel`, and every deploy.

After it commits I'll import the two accounts into `bootstrap`, apply `bootstrap`, then apply `infrastructure`, checking IAM between each given the clobbering we saw.
